Chapter 7: Healing the Wounds That Fuel Self-Sabotage.
As we move forward on this journey, there comes a point where we just can’t ignore those deeper wounds—the ones that quietly feed our self-sabotage. You know the kind I’m talking about: the old hurts, rejections, betrayals, and losses that stick around, often just below the surface.
These experiences don’t just fade away. They shape what we believe about ourselves, and how we behave—usually in ways we might not even notice. Healing isn’t about pretending the past never happened. It’s about finding a way to be at peace with it.
Picture this: someone who’s spent years in a cycle of failed relationships. Every time things start to get close, they pull away, or maybe even start an argument. Deep down, they want love more than anything. But those scars from old heartbreaks? They’ve made it feel risky to open up again.
The truth is, most of us carry wounds like this. Maybe it’s a child who grew up feeling invisible at home, and now struggles to trust their own worth as an adult. Or someone who was bullied or left out, and now has a hard time believing they truly belong anywhere. These moments leave a mark, shaping how we see ourselves, and the world around us.
Healing really starts with acknowledgment. Take the story of a man who always felt like an outsider. For years, he brushed off the pain of missing out on childhood friendships. But one day, he let himself sit with that sadness instead of just telling himself to “get over it.” It wasn’t comfortable, but something shifted. He started to feel compassion for his younger self, and slowly, he became more open to connecting with others.
Forgiveness is another powerful piece of this puzzle. And it’s not about excusing what happened or pretending it didn’t hurt. It’s about letting go of the hold those old wounds have on your present. For example, there was a woman who held onto resentment toward a parent for years. When she finally chose to forgive—not for them, but for herself—she realized she was setting herself free. The anger that weighed her down began to lift.
And here’s something most people miss: self-forgiveness matters just as much. It’s so easy to be hard on ourselves for mistakes we made, or things we wish we’d done differently. But if we want to heal, we have to let go of that shame, and start seeing ourselves with some kindness. The person who once sabotaged their own happiness can learn to recognize—they did the best they could with what they knew then.
Healing isn’t a straight line. Sometimes, old wounds come back up, especially when we’re stressed or feeling vulnerable. The key is to meet those moments with patience and compassion, and to trust that every small step forward truly counts.
As these wounds start to heal, something amazing happens. The urge to self-sabotage loses its grip. Your mind, no longer trapped by fear or old pain, is finally free to reach for growth, connection, and possibility. Suddenly, the mountain that once felt impossible to climb becomes a place of real healing—and even transformation.
